procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Munsiff Magistrate granting bail to the appellants before the expiry of 90 days of remand period allowed under law.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State filed a petition in the Andhra Pradesh High Court (Crl. Misc. Petition No. 4049 of 1985) for cancellation of the bail granted to the appellants. The High Court allowed the petition and cancelled the bail.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants-accused appealed to the Supreme Court against the judgment and order of the Andhra Pradesh High Court dated 31st December, 1985. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate is empowered to authorise the detention of an accused produced before him for a full period of 15 days from the date of production of the accused.

law.law_text: Section 167(2) of the Code empowers a Magistrate to "authorise the detention of the accused... for a term not exceeding 15 days in the whole".
Section 57 of the Code allows a police officer to detain an accused for up to 24 hours (plus journey time) before they must be produced before a Magistrate.

application.reasoning: The Court decided to apply the "plain meaning" of the words in Section 167(2), concluding that the 15-day period for which a Magistrate can authorize detention starts from the date the accused is produced before them.

The Court rejected the alternative argument that the 15-day period should be calculated from the date of arrest. It reasoned that this interpretation would require adding words to the statute that the legislature did not include, such as "from the date of arrest".

Calculating the period from the date of arrest would create practical difficulties. If an accused disputed the time of their arrest, the Magistrate would have to conduct a "fact finding inquiry" to determine the exact time, an exercise the Court found was not contemplated by the Code.

The Court pointed out an anomaly that would arise if the period was calculated from the date of arrest: the time the accused was in police custody before production (under Section 57) would have to be deducted from the 15 days. This would prevent the Magistrate from being able to authorize a full 15-day remand to either police or judicial custody.

The Court distinguished between custody under police power (before production) and detention authorized by a Magistrate. It stated that a Magistrate's authority to order detention only begins from the time the remand order is passed, and therefore the prior period in police custody is not included in the 15-day calculation.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a Magistrate is empowered to authorize the detention of an accused for a full period of 15 days, calculated from the date of the accused's production before the Magistrate, not from the date of arrest. This allows the Magistrate to place the accused in either police or judicial custody for the maximum period of 15 days from the date of the remand order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was right in allowing the petition filed by the State for cancellation of the bail granted to the appellants.

facts: The appellants were arrested on July 19, 1985, and produced before a Munsiff Magistrate on July 20, 1985, who remanded them to judicial custody.
The police filed a charge-sheet on October 17, 1985.

The Magistrate granted bail to the appellants, reasoning that the 90-day period for filing a charge-sheet under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure should be calculated from the date of arrest (July 19). By this calculation, the charge-sheet was filed on the 91st day, entitling them to bail.
The State challenged this order, and the High Court cancelled the bail, holding that the 90-day period must be computed from the date of remand (July 20).
law: The issue centered on the correct starting point for calculating the 90-day period of detention prescribed in the proviso to Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, after which an accused is entitled to default bail if a charge-sheet is not filed.
application: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' argument that the 90-day period should start from the date of arrest.

The Court affirmed the High Court's reasoning, holding that the 90-day period for detention under Section 167(2) must be computed from the date the accused is first remanded to custody by a Magistrate, not from the date of their arrest.
Applying this principle, the Court calculated that the charge-sheet, filed on October 17, 1985, was submitted on the 90th day of the remand period (which began on July 20, 1985).
Because the charge-sheet was filed within the legally allowed 90-day period, the appellants were not entitled to default bail.
Consequently, the Magistrate's order granting bail was incorrect, and the High Court was right to cancel it.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court upheld the High Court's decision to cancel the bail. It ruled that the 90-day period for filing a charge-sheet under Section 167(2) of the Code begins from the date of remand by a Magistrate, not the date of arrest. Since the charge-sheet was filed within this 90-day period, the appellants were not entitled to bail, and the Magistrate's order granting it was lawfully cancelled.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 10 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted to the facts of the case.

facts: The case involves the calculation of a total period of detention for an accused.
The Court referenced a precedent, Sureya Reddy's case, where the 90th day from the date of arrest was a Sunday.
law: Section 10 of the General Clauses Act, which addresses situations where the last day for performing an act is a holiday.

The precedent from Sureya Reddy's case, which held that Section 10 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted if the last day of a detention period is a holiday, and its principles should be invoked on considerations of justice and expediency.
application: The Court adopted the reasoning from Sureya Reddy's case.
It was noted that in the precedent case, the view was taken that Section 10 would apply if the last day was a Sunday or holiday.
The Court also considered the principle that the section should be invoked for reasons of justice and expediency.
Based on this, the Court stated it was "of the view that Section 10 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted that Section 10 of the General Clauses Act was attracted to the facts of the case, following the precedent and principles of justice established in Sureya Reddy's case.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate is empowered to authorise the detention of an accused produced before him for a full period of 15 days from the date of production of the accused.
appellant_arguments: The words 'for a term not exceeding 15 days in the whole' mean that the 15-day period must include any prior period of custody by a police officer before the accused was produced before the Magistrate.
The liberty of the citizen is a paramount consideration.
respondent_arguments: The period of detention is exclusively referable to the detentions ordered by a Magistrate and there is no scope for including any anterior period of custody by a police officer.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was right in allowing the petition filed by the State for cancellation of the bail granted to the appellants.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was wrong to cancel the bail. (Inferred from the action of appealing the High Court's judgment).
respondent_arguments: The High Court was correct in its judgment to cancel the bail. (Inferred from their position defending the High Court's judgment).

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 10 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted to the facts of the case.
appellant_arguments: Section 10 of the General Clauses Act is not applicable to the facts of the case. (Inferred, as applying the section was against their interest).
respondent_arguments: Section 10 of the General Clauses Act is applicable to the facts of the case. (Inferred, as the court's acceptance of this point supported the respondent's overall case).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A Magistrate is empowered to authorize the detention of an accused produced before him for a full period of 15 days from the date of production, as the words 'in the whole' in Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure govern the phrase 'for a term not exceeding 15 days'.
obiter: The intention of the Legislature can be gathered by comparing different subsections of the same statute; for instance, if the Legislature intended for the 90/60 day period in proviso (a) of Section 167(2) to be calculated from the date of arrest, it would have expressly stated so as it did in Section 167(5).
Section 10 of the General Clauses Act is applicable in relevant circumstances.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was correct to cancel the bail granted by the Munsiff Magistrate because the Magistrate had granted it before the expiry of the 90-day remand period allowed under law. The court's interpretation of related procedural rules, including the calculation of the 15-day initial detention period and the applicability of the General Clauses Act, supports the conclusion that the bail was granted prematurely and was therefore invalid.
legal_tests_applied: Interpretation of the phrase 'for a term not exceeding 15 days in the whole' under Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Application of Section 10 of the General Clauses Act to procedural deadlines in criminal law.
Interpretation of the conditions for granting default bail under the proviso (a) to Section 167(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, specifically the completion of the 90-day remand period.
why_appellant_lost: The court found 'no merit or force' in the contention that the words 'for a term not exceeding 15 days in the whole' in Section 167(2) should include any period of custody by a police officer before the accused was produced before the Magistrate.
The Munsiff Magistrate granted bail to the appellants 'before the expiry of 90 days of remand period allowed under law', making the bail order improper.
The court rejected the appellant's position by explicitly stating its view 'that Section 10 of the General Clauses Act would be attracted' to the facts of the case.
why_respondent_won: The High Court was correct in cancelling the bail because the Magistrate had granted it prematurely, before the legally mandated 90-day remand period had expired.
The court accepted the respondent's interpretation that the 15-day detention period authorized by a Magistrate is exclusive of any prior police custody.
The court affirmed the respondent's position by holding that Section 10 of the General Clauses Act was applicable to the calculation of the time period in this case.
policy_considerations: The proviso to Section 167 has been enacted not only to safeguard the liberty of the citizens but also 'to safeguard the interests of the State or in other words the public.'

The court corrected the notion from some previous decisions that the 'only factor underlying the legislative provision is the anxiety of the Legislature to safeguard the liberty of the citizen', emphasizing instead the dual concern for both individual liberty and public interest.
